article_text:
特別展「ベスト オブ すみだ北斎美術館―隅田川両岸景色図巻と名品―」

会場：すみだ北斎美術館（東京都墨田区亀沢２－７－２）

会期：２０２６年９月１５日（火）～１１月２３日（月、祝）

休館日：月曜休館、ただし９月２１日、１０月１２日、１１月２３日は開館し、９月２４日、１０月１３日が休館。１０月２０日は展示替えのため、特別展は休室。

開館時間：９：３０～１７：３０（入館は１７：００まで）

観覧料：一般１５００円、６５歳以上１０００円、高校生・大学生１０００円、中学生５００円、障がい者５００円、小学生以下無料

アクセス：ＪＲ両国駅東口から徒歩９分、都営地下鉄大江戸線両国駅Ａ３出口から徒歩５分

※前期（～１０月１８日）、後期（１０月２１日～）で展示替えあり ※１０月１日から、墨田区在住・在学の中学生は学生証などの提示で観覧料無料 ※詳細情報は 公式ホームページ で確認を

世界で最も有名な浮世絵師・葛飾北斎とその一門の作品を収集・展示するすみだ北斎美術館は今年11月、開館10周年を迎える。それを記念して、５人の学芸員がそれぞれ50作の「推し」を選び、前後期に分けて展示するのがこの「ベスト オブ すみだ北斎美術館」だ。あまりにも有名な「冨嶽三十六景」「諸国瀧廻り」などの錦絵から版本の挿絵、さらに肉筆画や弟子たちの作品に至るまで、北斎一門の画業を網羅した展覧会なのである。

展覧会は〈１章 北斎の肉筆画〉〈２章 北斎の錦絵〉〈３章 北斎の摺物〉〈４章 北斎の版本〉〈５章 魅力的な門人〉という構成。〈１章〉の最大の見どころ、今回の展覧会の目玉は、戯作者で落語家だった烏亭焉馬の依頼で北斎が描いた「隅田川両岸景色図巻」の詳細な解説だ。両国橋のあたりから吉原遊廓に向かって隅田川を遡る。その両岸の風景を、時間の経過を感じさせながら丁寧に描いている。最後の場面が上に挙げた図（後期展示）。真ん中で花魁たちに囲まれながら酒を飲んでいるのが、北斎自身なのだという説もある。

もう一つの見どころが、並んで展示されている「節季候図」と「雀と罠図」。両作品の表具などをすみだ北斎美術館で調べたところ、この２枚の絵は、かつてひとつの「押絵貼屏風」の一部だった可能性があるという。地道な調査で新たな発見が生まれることもあるのだ。

続く〈２章〉。北斎といえば千円札の裏側に採用されている「冨嶽三十六景 神奈川沖浪裏」が有名だが、それ以前から「波」の描写は何度も試みており、その１枚が下の「賀奈川沖本杢之図」。額縁のような枠の表現といい、西洋絵画の影響が見られる。「山下白雨」は「神奈川沖浪裏」「凱風快晴」と並ぶ「冨嶽三十六景」の「三名作」のひとつ。同館が所蔵するこのシリーズの中では特に「武州玉川」という作品の保存状態がいいそうで、後期でそれが展示される。

北斎が最初に入門したのは、役者絵・美人画の名手だった勝川春章で、若い頃はその門下で役者絵などを描いていたのだが、師匠の死後、兄弟子との不仲もあって勝川派を離れることになったといわれている。独立独歩となった北斎は、錦絵よりも摺物、読本挿絵の絵師として、まずは名を挙げたのである。〈これまた狂歌はいかゐ等の摺物画に名高く、浅草第六天神の脇町に住〉。江戸時代の浮世絵師たちの来歴を書いた『浮世絵類考』には、こんなことが記されている。『浮世絵類考』の底本ができたのは文政年間、1820年前後といわれており、「冨嶽三十六景」で北斎の錦絵が大ブレイクする約10年前。それまでは、こんな評価だったのである。

ちょっと長くなったが、こういう北斎の歩みを頭に入れておくと、〈３章〉〈４章〉の価値が分かってくる。ちなみに「摺物」とは趣味人やそのグループが自分たちでお金を出して制作する「私家版」の浮世絵。今で言えば、「年賀状」みたいなものだろうか。そんなものだから、「錦絵」よりもマニアックだったり細部に凝っていたりしていて、また違った味わいがあるのである。〈４章〉で展示される版本、特に馬琴と組んだ『椿説弓張月』などの読本の挿絵は、スケール雄大で迫力満点。下に挙げたのは、雪国の生活を物語的に描いた『北越奇談』だが、当時は無名だった作者の崑崙を売り出すため、版元が挿絵の名手・北斎を起用したとも言われている。

版本挿絵、摺物、錦絵、肉筆画･･････浮世絵の様々なジャンルで大きな足跡を残した北斎には、数多くの弟子がいた。その作品を集めたのが〈５章〉。実は北斎という名跡は、二代目・三代目もいたようで、「二代目」の作品も後期では展示される。弟子の中には今では経歴不明となっている存在もいて、「三美人」を描いた天淵道人はその代表格。このほか、西洋画の影響を受けたちょっと奇妙な風景画を描く昇亭北寿、狂歌摺物や美人画で有名な蹄斎北馬、もともとは四谷鮫ヶ橋で鮮魚商を営んでいたという魚屋北溪らの作品が並んでいる。

ふたつのフロアを使った今回の企画、ご覧の通り、とにかく豪華な内容。何しろ、５章それぞれで、ひとつの展覧会を開くことができるだけの所蔵品をすみだ北斎美術館は所持しているのだから。開館当時、すみだ北斎美術館には約1800点の所蔵品があったそうで、その数は開館後も増えているという。その中から厳選した「ベスト・オブ・ベスト」を見せてくれるこの展覧会、北斎とは何者か、その一門にはどんな特徴があるのか、それを分かりやすく見せてくれる、浮世絵初心者にも優しい構成なのである。（美術展ナビ取材班 田中聡）

article_text:
Bristol Photo Festival’s third edition creates a palimpsest of past, present and future, explains festival director Alejandro Acín

In Castle Park, central Bristol, there is a plaque paying tribute to men from the city who joined the fight against fascism in the Spanish Civil War. “It’s always been in my mind,” says Bristol Photo Festival director Alejandro Acín. This year marks 90 years since the Spanish Civil War but, with authoritarian governments and far-right activism rising across the globe, that moment now feels uncomfortably close.

It is a reminder that the past has a way of shapeshifting into the present, and this idea reverberates through the 2026 Bristol Photo Festival. Themed Time Machine , it includes a show taking place in a cave not far from the park featuring three artists exploring the contemporary resonance of the Spanish Civil War – Anna Jorné, Julián Barón and Natasha Christia. Their work is part of a city-wide programme of exhibitions in which photography is not simply a recording of the past, but an articulation of our non-linear experience of time. Memory of what has been and speculation about the future meet in the present day.

“Often the works that we bring explore historical events but from contemporary approaches, or vice versa, so there’s always this kind of entanglement of time that happens,” Acín notes, adding that Time Machine follows two previous editions focusing on movement (in 2024) and place (in 2021). “We can look at the three editions as almost a trilogy,” he explains.

“Culture this year is more political than ever. We are fighting to keep spaces that allow people to think, talk and look at the world differently” – Alejandro Acín

This year a show by Goa-based artist Akshay Mahajan responds to the British Empire and Commonwealth Collection held in Bristol, drawing on Indian folklore to consider how the ghosts of colonialism still haunt the border between India and Pakistan. Italian photojournalist Giulio Di Sturco’s Anthropocosmos invites viewers into constructed spaces designed by scientists and engineers, meanwhile, to test out space conditions. His images show how humans are preparing for a potential – as yet unrealised – future beyond Earth.

There is also an exhibition presented by Kegham Djeghalian, the son of the late Kegham Avedis Garabet Djeghalian – an Armenian-Palestinian photographer who set up Gaza’s first photographic studio. Djeghalian Senior’s images are a portal to a flourishing pre-Nakba Palestine, which stands in stark contrast to the horrifying images of destruction of recent years. Elsewhere Annie Wang’s Mother as a Creator charts the Taiwanese artist’s journey into pregnancy, through motherhood, and on to the shifting, overlapping terrain she now occupies between her maternal and creative roles.

This edition of Bristol Photo Festival is Acín’s second as director (after a stint as director of education and engagement for the first edition); alongside it he runs IC Visual Lab with co-director Ben GJ Thomas and designer/producer Safia Belhaj. ICVL is based in the middle of the city, in the one-time home of the South African Resource Centre and curator Christine Eyene is drawing on the building’s radical history for an exhibition there, featuring work by George Hallett. An award-winning South African photographer, Hallett was exiled to London in the 1970s and made portraits of anti-apartheid creatives, writers, artists and musicians.

The festival includes a busy opening week from 14 to 18 October, featuring parties, openings and a symposium; it will also include an ‘education weekend’ in its five-week run, featuring masterclasses led by photographers and industry insiders. “It’s about building relationships where participants can continue developing their work,” says Acín.

The 2024 festival was a resounding success. Amak Mahmoodian’s exhibition in it, One Hundred and Twenty Minutes , went on to earn a Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize nomination, while some 40 per cent of those who went to the Bristol Museum and Art Gallery during its run were visiting the institution for the first time. “We had visitors from every postcode in Bristol, so on a local level we had pretty good engagement,” says Acín.

However, since then much has changed in Bristol (and beyond), with arts organisations facing a tougher funding landscape than ever. Bristol Photo Festival consists of curated exhibitions – rather than depending on an open call – which provides an income for some; this puts more financial pressure on the festival, and more onus on partnership. The closure of the Royal Photographic Society’s gallery has also had an impact, as it was previously a key venue – although some new spaces have come on board.

The festival, along with the wider photography community, is also still mourning the loss of Martin Parr in December 2025, a long-term Bristol resident and keen advocate of the programme. “It was very sad,” says Acín. “Martin was part of the board and he was always helpful with contacts, interested and supportive of the festival.” The festival maintains close ties with the Martin Parr Foundation, whose group exhibition Dark Tales: British Documentary Photography and the Gothic will be on show during its run; the popular Books on Photography will also return to MPF on 17 and 18 October.

Acín is open about the difficulties, believing it is important for organisations to speak up about the impact of massive cuts to public arts in the UK, and the loss of access to EU funding post-Brexit. “It’s a reality that’s very palpable, very tangible,” he says. “Culture this year is more political than ever. We are fighting to keep spaces that allow people to think, talk and look at the world differently.”

Bristol Photo Festival takes place from 14 October–15 November 2026. BOP is the weekend of 17–18 October 2026.

Rachel Segal Hamilton is a freelance writer and editor, specialising in photography and visual culture, for art magazines, book publishers, national press, awards, agencies and brands. Since 2018, she’s been contributing editor for the Royal Photographic Society Journal, is a regular writer for Aesthetica and author of Unseen London, published by Hoxton Mini Press.

article_text:
Art Review

John Dilg’s Down-to-Earth Reverence

The tranquility of his views, the closeness of his tones, and the evenness of his light bespeak his continual wonderment at existence.

John Dilg’s paintings don’t seem to have undergone any seismic changes during the decade I’ve been following his work, so I wasn’t sure there was anything else I could say about it. But after visiting a recent exhibition at Peter Freeman Gallery and reflecting on my experience, I realized I was wrong.

The show included 13 paintings, 10 of which were made this year. Twelve measured 14 x 18 1/8 inches (~35.6 x 46 cm) and were oriented horizontally or vertically. The circumscribed palette of pale blues, celadon greens, browns, and off-white was present in every work, and the application was unvaried; the nub of the canvas was visible through the thin layer of paint. In addition to oil paint, Dilg used charcoal and graphite to draw the contour of his unmistakable natural forms. Except for “Wild Life” (2024), the subject of each painting is a spare, serene landscape with almost no signs of human life, often under a full moon blanketing the world in perpetual twilight. For the sameness in size, palette, and application, Dilg did not repeat himself.

Left: John Dilg, "Bloom Watch" (2026), oil, charcoal, and graphite on canvas; right: John Dilg, "Sequoia" (2026), oil, charcoal, and graphite on canvas

2027年1⽉31⽇より、郡⼭市⽴美術館にて写真家・柴田敏雄の展覧会を開催する。

柴⽥敏雄（1949−）は東京藝術⼤学、同⼤学⼤学院で油彩画と版画を学んだのち、ベルギーのゲント市王⽴アカデミーに留学。留学をきっかけに写真による制作を開始した柴⽥は、帰国後の1980年代後半以降、ダムや擁壁といった構造物が作り出す⼈⼯的な景観を重厚なモノクローム写真に定着させる作品を制作。1992年に展覧会「⽇本典型」などによって第17回⽊村伊兵衛写真賞を受賞。⼤型カメラの持つ精緻な描写⼒と厳密な画⾯構成によって⽣み出された作品は、⼈⼯物と⾃然が共存する景観を緻密に捉えつつ、抽象的な造形美を描出し、国際的に⾼く評価されている。2007年以降はカラー写真へと表現の軸を移し、さらなる展開がなされている。代表作「⽇本典型」をはじめ、その作品群には東北の⾵景を捉えたものも数多く含まれるが、柴⽥は幼少期の⼀時期を福島県の会津で過ごしていた。ゆかりのある地域において初の開催となる⼤規模な展覧会は、⼤きな意味を持つことになるだろう。

国内美術館19 年ぶりの個展となる本展覧会では、初期から現在に⾄るまでの作品を精選し、約50年のキャリアに及ぶ作家の軌跡をたどる。 会期中には作家を交えたクロストークや学芸員によるギャラリーツアーなどイベントも豊富。この機会にぜひご高覧いただきたい。

article_text:
“ Whalefall ” asks how much patience you can sustain for discussing your friend’s daddy issues while also actively trying to help them escape being devoured by a literal whale. The answer, in director Brian Duffield ’s at-once brutal and sincere survival thriller , is less than you might hope.

There’s plenty to unpack about the troubled relationship between young scuba diver Jay Gardiner ( Austin Abrams ) and his late father Mitt ( Josh Brolin ). But by chance, have you considered just how rapidly gallons of digestive fluid might rip away human skin?

Adapted by Duffield and Daniel Kraus from Kraus’ 2023 novel, this spectacularly unpleasant underwater adventure delivers on its premise with effects that are graphic, fascinating, and occasionally beautiful. It also keeps interrupting that accomplishment to explain why being swallowed by a sperm whale is emotionally significant. You would think the whale had that covered.

Mitt’s seaside death opens the film and a year later, Jay heads into the ocean looking for his father’s remains — compelled by an obligation he can’t quite explain. A squid soon complicates the excursion, drawing him into the path of a feeding whale and then into the animal itself. That’s already one more creature than the metaphor strictly needs, but Duffield makes the encounter haunting. Before Jay becomes lunch, he sees the sperm whale in all its glory and he knows exactly how big the problem is.

Fresh off Zach Cregger’s “Resident Evil,” Abrams remains the kind of actor you perpetually want to root for, and his muffled screams through a scuba breathing apparatus are especially terrifying. Against his soft, sensitive frame, this underwater world looks impossibly hard. Toxic air and bubbling yellow acid turn the whale’s interior into a washing machine of physical injury and psychological torment, and Jay will regret diving without his gloves way, way more than he knows.

The effects are exceptional, but it’s the awareness Abrams brings to this predicament that really makes them hurt. Resting his head against some whale intestine while working the problem, he briefly evokes storybook illustrations suggesting a person could really make a home there. Then the flesh inexplicably ripples around him, reminding us whose home this actually is. For all its spiritual ambitions, “Whalefall” rarely lets you forget that its protagonist is inside an animal — and that’s mostly to the film’s benefit.

Thank God there’s some trash in the whale, too. It gives Jay materials to work with, while bioluminescent creatures provide light and a strangely ethereal atmosphere. And a jellyfish becomes something like Wilson from “Cast Away,” albeit with less obvious sporting potential. These luminous interludes also ease us into the memories of Jay’s father that keep intruding on his predicament. Sometimes, a flashback is a welcome reprieve. (God knows you don’t want anything else to happen to this kid.)

Mostly, however, the cutting is jarring. The past and present compete for attention without consistently making each other more interesting, and the escape-room mechanics suffer from a peculiar combination of overexplanation and confusion. Despite Duffield’s skill with minimal dialogue in “No One Will Save You,” Jay frequently announces what we can already see. He coughs, then explains that the air is poisonous. Even oxygen updates are delivered aloud to an audience of stomach contents.

Meanwhile, the geography that would help us understand his decisions remains frustratingly vague. Beyond distinguishing the gross green part from the super fucking scary yellow part, navigating the interior of the whale almost requires a Discovery Channel overlay. Some punishing sequences are difficult to appreciate as physical problems because it’s unclear where Jay is or what movement might accomplish. Too often, “Whalefall” explains the obvious and leaves the complicated stuff floating.

Much of the instruction arrives through remembered lessons from good ol’ Dad, whose wisdom becomes both a survival resource and a reason to reconsider him. But knowing something about the ocean doesn’t necessarily make a man a good father, and the script keeps reaching for those pearls of wisdom as if their practical usefulness might settle something about their history. That’s a lot to ask of scuba advice.

Brolin’s character mocked his son, called him “soft lungs,” and said frightening things when drunk. His death from mesothelioma leaves plenty for Jay to process. The problem isn’t that the kid hasn’t suffered enough to deserve a movie. Rather, it’s that the flashbacks don’t make this particular father and son compelling enough to keep pulling us out of the whale.

Covered in nautical tattoos and given to spiritual proclamations about the ocean’s generosity, Mitt is recognizable as a type. But Brolin and Abrams struggle to feel like members of the same family, and Jay has little identity outside their conflict. An out-of-state scholarship suggests a future, but scarcely defines the person who might live it. When Brolin’s voice takes on a ghostly presence inside the whale, the emotional insistence grows louder without becoming more persuasive.

There’s something intriguing in that slipperiness. His dad is the whale, but his dad is also his dad, and the whale is also… a whale. Like Jonah, Jay confronts the possibility that divine will, fate, or whatever governs the universe cannot be outrun. Then again, the creature’s indifference suggests there may be no deeper meaning available. That tension gives Duffield more to work with than the familiar monster-as-grief metaphor, even when he struggles to make it coherent.

For comparison, Mike Flanagan’s “Gerald’s Game” faced a related challenge, threading traumatic memories of an abusive marriage through an immediate survival problem. There, the psychological story energized a bedroom where the protagonist could barely move. Here, an entire ecosystem is already happening. Asking viewers to contemplate childhood pain while monitoring digestion requires two kinds of attention that Duffield only intermittently brings together.

When he does, the results are extraordinary. A pressure-related assault on Jay’s sinuses explodes into a memory of fireworks, a transition as beautiful as it is horrible. Likewise, a sequence involving orcas reveals a filmmaker capable of making this ocean feel moving and immense. These passages connect sensation and emotion without stopping to explain their relationship. Of course, they also make the surrounding imbalance more frustrating. So does the puzzle’s payoff.

Armed with a trash bag, an old sock, scuba equipment, and more emotional baggage than you could package in a semester-long underwater basket-weaving class, Jay seems equipped to impress us with his ingenuity. Instead, too much of the process resembles making peace with your past and developing marine communication powers akin to Aquaman. There is a practical component, but it struggles to compete with the therapeutic one.

After everything Jay endures, you want the satisfaction of watching him work the problem of a damn whale. Instead, you’re seeing him move through the digestive tract of a screenplay, where emotional breakthroughs carry an awkward amount of physiological authority.

More of the horror-comedy sensibility Duffield brought to “Spontaneous” might have helped this material breathe. Still, the sincerity matters, and so does the achievement of realizing something this strange with such conviction. Even when the metaphor is painfully on the nose, the film’s most disturbing images are more than their dramatic limitations and a whale is still an astonishing place to spend a movie.

“Whalefall” isn’t always sure what it wants to add to the mythology of these creatures: Are we afraid of what whales can do to us, or ashamed of what we have done to them? Its father-son drama doesn’t settle the matter. But Duffield does contribute something to the conversation, and it’s worth appreciating on its own terms… as a dude (and his very literary trauma!) stuck inside an actual whale.

Grade: B-

From 20th Century Studios, “Whalefall” is in theaters Friday, October 16.

15世紀から16世紀にかけて隆盛を極めたルネサンス芸術。中心にいたのが天才レオナルド・ダ・ヴィンチです。パリ・ルーヴル美術館にはダ・ヴィンチの絵画が5枚収蔵されていますが、「モナ・リザ」から実に50年以上を経て初来日を果たしたのが、「女性の肖像」別称「美しきフェロニエール」です。この絵にはダ・ヴィンチが試みた肖像画革命が凝縮されていました。

今回イタリアの美術史家や美術解剖学の第一人者の視点から絵を徹底分析！今では当たり前に思われている肖像画のポージングや表現が、実はダ・ヴィンチの生み出したものであることが明らかに。そしてあの「モナ・リザ」の謎めいた姿の秘密も…？真矢ミキさんが挑みます。

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班）

article_text:
Double Oscar nominee James Longley , who won the top award at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival on Saturday with “ Mohabat ,” will focus next on the Rohingya genocide.

Longley – who was Oscar nominated for “Iraq in Fragments” and “Sari’s Mother” – tells Variety at the Czech event, “I’ve already filmed act one of this project, working with Diane Weyermann [ who died in 2021 ] at Participant Media, when they were still around [the company was shut down in 2024]. Next year marks the 10th anniversary of the 2017 genocide.”

He adds, “[It’s] a genocide that’s formally recognized as such by the United States, the EU and the British government, yet, surprisingly, no documentary feature has been produced on this subject. I’m uniquely prepared to make that film.”

Longley doesn’t mind being an outsider. His latest, “Mohabat,” is set in Afghanistan.

“I’m not attempting to become Afghan. I’m trying to help non-Afghans understand Afghanistan better. After fighting a war in their country for 20 years, this seems like the least we can do,” he says.

He arrived “with a camera in my hand instead of a gun” and was treated as a guest, not an enemy.

“I went to their country with the sincere goal of telling their stories, so I was accepted and afforded patience.

“I cannot describe what an honor it has been for me to live and work alongside the Afghan people, who are brave and pure of heart in a way most Americans could take a good lesson from.”

His protagonist, 12-year-old Mohabat, tries to hold his family together under Taliban rule after a U.S. drone kills his father while he’s out hunting.

“This happened during the first Trump administration, when Mike Pompeo was in charge of the drone program,” says Longley.

“During the 20-year war, such events were common and untold numbers of civilians were killed and forgotten far from the foreign journalists in Kabul. Mohabat did not want his father to be forgotten, and so he stuck with us patiently throughout two years of filming.”

During location scouting, the team visited orphanages filled with children who had lost their parents in the war.

“The sons of Afghan policemen martyred in Taliban suicide bombings share their bread with the sons of martyred Taliban fighters. Many of them wanted to tell their stories. That was never an issue,” he says.

“Mohabat believed that we would do justice to the memory of his father, a poor man with a wife and seven children, who worked as a tea seller in a large market on the edge of Kabul.”

He adds: “Elham, one of Mohabat’s friends, told us specifically that he was waiting for a foreign journalist to come and talk to them about what they had seen during the war and what they thought about it.”

Longley is no stranger to making films “about young people and for young people,” such as “Iraq in Fragments,” “Angels Are Made of Light” and now “Mohabat.”

“When we are children, we experience the world most directly – and for the first time. When I direct a documentary in Afghanistan, Iraq or Gaza and show it to a Western audience, I know I’m taking them to a new place. In this situation, it’s most appropriate to give them a child’s perspective because [they’re] like a child in those countries, experiencing something new.

“I’ve included many adults in my documentaries, but most audience members never remember them after watching the film.”

He’s influenced by Vittorio De Sica, Abbas Kiarostami, Majid Majidi, François Truffaut and other directors who “treat the lives of their child characters with great seriousness.”

“This can also work in documentaries,” he emphasizes. Especially when working in a “restrictive space.”

“Making a film in Afghanistan, either during the war or under the Taliban, with a child as the main protagonist doesn’t make the job more difficult; it makes it much easier. You’ll get permission to make a film about a kid a 100 times before you will get permission to make a film about an adult.”

He wasn’t able to film women, however.

“It would have caused a local scandal if one of the village women had appeared in our film. She would never have been able to live it down. The issue is not whether women can talk; it’s more that their neighbors would never stop talking about it,” he observes.

“Plenty of Afghan women are making their own films in secret on their iPhones, so I didn’t feel it was necessary to duplicate their efforts. I’m in no position to make a film about Afghan women, and meanwhile, Afghan women filmmakers are in no position to make the kind of film we made in ‘Mohabat.’”

He ended up joining forces with Alex Gibney , who is credited as a producer alongside Longley and Mohammad Sharif Hotak.

“Alex saw ‘Angels Are Made of Light’ and liked it. When I asked him if he would like to produce a film with me about life in Afghanistan under the Taliban, he immediately said yes.

“It’s been a joy working with him, mostly because he’s the best documentary producer alive and also a deeply intelligent person. This kind of collaboration and level of trust is a dream for any filmmaker.”

He also praises Hotak, who lived just down the road from the villages where they filmed.

“His familiarity with the place and the people was the key to making the movie. He grew up experiencing the same realities of war as the children in the film, so he could relate to them directly.”

Finding a personal angle is crucial for Longley, regardless of where he’s heading.

“I see all films and media as reflecting the politics around which they were made and the politics of those who made them. Corporate news media make products that aligns with the politics of their owners and advertisers. I make films that reflect my own politics, which are pro-human and anti-war,” he notes.

“I suspect that my films are in direct conflict with almost everything you will see on television, but I can’t say for sure – I’ve never owned a TV. I don’t care about what most of those people have to say.”

article_text:
Four years ago this week , James Gunn and Peter Safran were handed one of Hollywood’s most coveted, and impossible, jobs. When they were named co-CEOs of Warner Bros.’ DC Studios label, they received complete oversight of comic book characters like Superman, Wonder Woman, Batman* (more on that later), Green Lantern, the Flash, and countless others. With a seemingly blank canvas to make as many movies and shows as their hearts desired, the implied mandate was clear: get DC Comics out of second place.

The studio’s DC division spent much of the 2010s as a laughingstock while its Marvel competitors seemed to never miss. Despite having a better roster of characters — 20 years ago, mentioning the Guardians of the Galaxy in the same breath as Batman would have been laughable even to the biggest comic book nerd — Warner Bros. couldn’t figure out how to turn its characters into must-see cinema. The incredible cultural moment of the Christopher Nolan Batman movies gave way to one misfire after another: Zack Snyder’s “Man of Steel” gave way to the “Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice” debacle, Patty Jenkins’ acclaimed “Wonder Woman” movie led to a critically panned sequel, and the studio’s attempt to launch its own “Avengers” with “Justice League” was bad enough to leave fans arguing about different cuts instead of wondering where the story went next.

It was the kind of turnaround project that entitles its leaders to a long runway. After Gunn and Safran accepted the job in late 2022, they began announcing projects in early 2023. Then they had to shoot and edit them, meaning that we didn’t really see the vision take shape until this year. But now we’ve seen Gunn and Safran release three major theatrical films, two live-action shows, and multiple animated ones — more than enough of a sample size to start grading their creative direction. Even if we’re still in Phase One of their long-term plan, the pros and cons of their studio approach are becoming clear.

The Films

Gunn and Safran kicked off their DC tenure with the safest and smartest film they could have possibly made: a “Superman” movie written and directed by Gunn himself . Putting DC’s signature character in the hands of a filmmaker with an unimpeachable ability to deliver smart popcorn fare was a no-brainer. And in many ways, “Superman” delivered.

The film wisely skipped the obligatory origin story that everyone already knows, checking in with the man formerly known as Kal-El after he had already assumed his dual role of Superman and Clark Kent on Earth. Gunn brought his signature blend of heart, humor, and needle drops, delivering an entertaining blockbuster that stood in clear contrast to the excessively dark DC films of the 2010s. This movie was colorful and fun, even in its heaviest moments. Unsurprisingly, it grossed over $600 million worldwide — though it still didn’t tell us much about Gunn’s ability to run a studio. His bona fides as a comic book writer/director were never in doubt, but we still hadn’t seen him supervise other filmmakers.

Those opportunities came in 2026, and the results were more polarizing. The studio’s second film, “Supergirl,” was one of the year’s most public flops. Milly Alcock’s eponymous character appeared briefly in “Superman,” but Craig Gillespie’s film traded its predecessor’s grounded Earth drama for a space western set across a series of “Mad Max”-esque planets. The confusing mythology and grating visual effects felt like a departure, and the film received mixed reviews and only made $100 million worldwide despite costing nearly twice that. Equally concerning were reports about creative clashes between Gunn and Safran and Gillespie, with two competing cuts being screened against each other months before the movie opened.

Then came “ Clayface .” James Watkins’ origin story for an obscure Batman villain was branded as a horror movie that just happened to exist within a comic book universe. The gory, goopy story of an actor who sacrifices everything to regain his skin-deep beauty wasn’t for everyone , but it represented a real creative swing. And it was made on a responsible $44 million budget, which removed the pressure to be universally appealing.

It’s easy to see a world where this DC universe thrives with a combination of major tentpoles directed by Gunn (who is already hard at work on a “Superman” follow-up dated for July 2027) and smaller, weirder films based on minor characters. But we still haven’t seen Gunn and Safran oversee a blockbuster that connects with mainstream audiences with another filmmaker in the director’s chair. “Supergirl” may end up being an anomaly, but right now it still represents one-third of their theatrical output. That sadly has to count for something.

Grade: B –

The Shows

Gunn and Safran’s overhaul of DC’s TV output technically began before they took over as CEOs, as “Peacemaker” premiered on HBO Max nine months earlier. Created (and largely directed) by Gunn, the raunchy action comedy saw John Cena reprising his role from Gunn’s “Suicide Squad” movie as an antihero willing to kill as many men, women, and children as he needs to achieve his goal of world peace. Gunn’s sensibilities were still there, but the HBO brand let the show include far more nudity and profanity than you’d ever find in a four-quadrant film. A hit with fans and critics, “Peacemaker” reminded audiences what was possible when you had access to a premium cable brand to complement your theatrical films.

Their first official project after taking the reins was also a TV show. The animated “Creature Commandos” debuted on HBO Max in December 2024 with an inoffensive six-episode Season 1 that showcased Gunn’s favorite themes about weirdos who assemble their own found families. The business stakes were low — fairly or not, the average consumer isn’t watching animated superhero shows, and the diehard fans who do tune in are unlikely to ever stop supporting DC’s other projects. But the series has one notable wrinkle: Gunn cast its voice actors with the intention of reprising their roles in live-action projects, a tactic he says he plans to use on all future animated projects.

“Peacemaker” also concluded with a well-received Season 2, but the real test of the DC Universe’s TV output came this fall with “Lanterns.” Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof, and Tom King’s series about DC’s intergalactic police force more than delivered on its promise to be “True Detective” with Green Lanterns. The film uses classic police procedural tropes — the show centers on an older, set-in-his-ways Green Lantern who reluctantly partners with a talented young partner he won’t give the time of day to — in a dark, season-long murder saga set in middle America. The show itself received rave reviews , but its actual contents matter less than what it represents: a unique, auteur-driven project that fits into Gunn and Safran’s storyline while allowing other filmmakers to showcase their own voices. So far, it’s the ultimate example of what the CEOs have always said they wanted their DC Studios to do.

Grade: A-

The Batman Problem

Perhaps the biggest variable facing Gunn and Safran’s DC Studios is largely outside their control. Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” had already opened in theaters a few months before they took over, and Warner Bros. announced that the Robert Pattinson-led series would continue separately from the new DC Universe. A second film is in production, with Steven Soderbergh helping to complete principal photography , and HBO shows like “The Penguin” and the recently announced “Poison Ivy” continue to expand the mythology.

Gunn and Safran have some involvement in these “Batman” projects and publicly support them, but the films and shows exist outside the overarching storyline they’re trying to build. And while it’s not an insurmountable problem — multiple artists working with the same characters in different timelines has been a trademark of comic books from the very beginning — it’s also not ideal to have one of your franchise’s two biggest characters tied up outside your purview.

Nothing’s stopping Gunn and Safran from bringing in their own Batman, and it seems inevitable that it will happen soon. “Clayface” takes place in Gotham City, and once you start introducing Batman villains, you need to give audiences something to fight them. Gunn and Safran previously tapped Andy Muschietti to direct a Batman movie called “The Brave and the Bold,” which was still in development as of 2025 , but no cast or release date has been announced.

Many fans and Warner Bros. shareholders believe this DC Universe won’t reach its full potential until it introduces its own Batman. The kind of major team-up movies with billion-dollar box office potential, like a new “Justice League” or a “World’s Finest” team-up between Batman and Superman, all feature the Dark Knight. And assuming their Batman isn’t Robert Pattinson, they’ll inevitably be faced with audiences who wonder why or see theirs as a second-tier product.

It’s not fair to grade Gunn and Safran on this problem, since they didn’t create it, but they still have to navigate it. Again, it’s not insurmountable, but Kevin Feige never had to deal with this at Marvel.

Grade: N/A

The Process

Gunn and Safran’s overarching DC story is still in its infancy, but their development process has become clear. And it’s arguably their best asset. In many ways, their DC Studios can be described as the anti-MCU. Whereas their competitor (and Gunn’s former employer) became famous for seeing everything as part of a larger puzzle, DC Studios seems much more focused on treating each film as a standalone project. Films are greenlit based on the quality of their individual scripts, not the Easter eggs that connect them. Nobody would ever tell you that a brand-new DC cinematic universe should release “Clayface” as one of its first films, but Gunn has openly said Mike Flanagan’s script stood out among the many other projects they were developing. The script was ready; therefore, they made the movie.

Prioritizing scripts over corporate synergy should be music to the ears of cinephiles burned out on Marvel’s assembly-line approach to storytelling. That means continuity will never be as tight as what you find in the MCU, and plenty of projects will be announced without ever coming to fruition. (We’re still upset about James Mangold’s “Swamp Thing” and Luca Guadagnino’s “Sgt. Rock” falling through the cracks, but it’s better than rushing out movies that aren’t ready.) Comic book fans used to following these companies like sports teams might need to adjust their expectations, but movie lovers who care less about those details should get richer viewing experiences. It’s also better for the creatives who get a chance to pitch their own original ideas and put their own stamp on beloved characters.

The only thing holding this back from an “A” grade is the fact that ideals that sound good on paper still have to be executed. I deeply admire Gunn for publicly declaring that no DC Studios movie will receive a release date until everyone is happy with the script. But I also saw “Supergirl” and wondered what this mysterious great script could have possibly looked like, and why it apparently didn’t make it into the finished movie.

Grade: B+

iTravelPoetry invites photographers worldwide to submit work for Beyond Borders , an international photography exhibition exploring geographical, cultural, social and personal boundaries. Selected photographs will be exhibited in Athens, Paris and Rome.

Open Call:

iTravelPoetry has announced an international open call for Beyond Borders , a photography exhibition bringing together photographic perspectives from around the world across three European cities.

The exhibition invites photographers to investigate the visible and invisible boundaries that shape human experience, examining how borders influence identity, memory, relationships and perceptions of the world.

The theme encompasses geographical, cultural, social, emotional and personal boundaries, encouraging participants to question the divisions that separate individuals and communities, as well as the connections that extend beyond them.

Photographers working across documentary, conceptual, fine art, street, portrait, landscape, abstract and experimental photography are invited to interpret the theme through their individual visual languages.

Selected photographs will be presented in Athens, Greece; Paris, France; and Rome, Italy, as part of a shared international exhibition.

Institutional Context:

iTravelPoetry is an independent cultural organisation dedicated to literature, cinema and contemporary artistic expression.

Through exhibitions, festivals, publications and audiovisual productions, the organisation creates opportunities for artists and cultural practitioners to present their work and engage with audiences.

Beyond Borders forms part of its programme of cultural initiatives, bringing together international photographic practices through exhibitions across multiple locations.

The project aims to present different perspectives on contemporary experience while encouraging artistic engagement with questions of identity, connection and boundaries.

Eligibility and Criteria:

The open call welcomes photographers from all countries, regardless of nationality, professional experience or artistic background.

Applicants must meet the following requirements:

Be aged 18 years or older.

Submit original photographic works created by the applicant.

Work in any photographic genre, style or technique.

Submit up to three photographs for consideration.

Provide each photograph as a separate JPG file with its own title.

Include their full name, country of residence, photograph title and year of creation.

Both emerging and established photographers are eligible.

No restrictions apply to photographic techniques or artistic approaches, as long as submitted works are original and respond to the exhibition’s open theme.

Evaluation Process:

The iTravelPoetry organising team will review submitted photographs.

Selection is not guaranteed, and applicants will be informed if their work has been chosen for the exhibition.

Successful applicants will receive further information concerning participation confirmation and practical arrangements.

A participation fee of €150 will apply only to selected photographers who choose to confirm their involvement.

The published announcement does not specify the composition of the selection committee, detailed assessment criteria or the date on which successful applicants will be notified.

Organiser: iTravelPoetry

Exhibition locations:

Athens, Greece

Paris, France

Rome, Italy

Application period: 17 October to 30 November 2026

Application deadline: 30 November 2026

Application fee: Free

Participation fee: €150, payable only upon selection and confirmation of participation.

Maximum submissions: Three photographs per applicant.

The €150 participation fee covers organisational expenses associated with presenting the selected work in all three cities. No separate participation fee applies for each exhibition location.

Every selected photograph will be included in all three exhibitions.

Specific exhibition dates and venue details will be announced after the submission period closes and the participation process is complete.

Country of residence.

Opinion

In Battle Over Auschwitz Watercolors, Roma Victims Are Getting Left Behind

As the legal dispute over the paintings’ ownership continues, no one seems to be asking: What were their names? Who may still be grieving their deaths? What decision would best honor them?

PACER )

The decades-long ownership dispute between the family of late Holocaust survivor Dina Gottliebova Babbitt and the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum over seven watercolors depicting Roma prisoners is back in the news . That's because the dispute culminated in a California lawsuit initiated by her daughters 17 years after their mother's death.

Nicknamed the “Angel of Death,” Dr. Josef Mengele ordered Babbitt to portray the traits of Roma prisoners as part of his pseudo-scientific experiments to prove what he perceived as their racial inferiority. Under these extreme life-and-death circumstances, Babbitt created the watercolors to save her life as well as her mother's. All the Roma people forced to pose for these portraits were later executed.

The news coverage and conversations around the ownership dispute have long missed an essential frame through which to view this tragedy: the rights and dignity of the Roma people who were depicted, killed, and forgotten. What decision would best honor them? How do we stop the harmful experiment's long-term impact from further stigmatizing Roma identity?

article_text:
It’s hard to imagine the American Film Institute ‘s board of directors without Bob Daly , but that will be the case as of next week. The former CBS and Warner Bros boss is stepping down after 17 years as its chairman — and 45 as a trustee.

Daly, who first joined the board in 1981, will exit the top post at the October 21 board meeting, where a successor will be discussed.

“In a career that brought me from running CBS to Warner Bros to the Los Angeles Dodgers, I can honestly say that serving as Chairman of the AFI Board of Directors has been one of the greatest honors of my career,” Daly said in a statement. “This is a board that represents all aspects of the film and television communities, and to see they come together with a shared passion for the art form has been a wonder to behold. Long live the AFI.”

A rep for AFI said Daly, who joined the board in April 1981, is stepping down to pass the torch to the next generation.

The pair were credited with 16 consecutive years of record earnings. Daly then was chairman and CEO of the Dodgers, the MLB team then-owned by News Corp. He also was chairman of the Save the Children board for five years.

“Leadership is an art in itself – and in that regard, Mr. Daly is a master,” AFI President and CEO Bob Gazzale said. “Over the past 40 years, no single person has had a greater impact on AFI’s work in preservation, celebration and education than Bob Daly.”

article_text:
“Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, is a once-in-a-lifetime gathering of more 120 works by America’s most storied art couple: Lee Krasner (1908–84) and Jackson Pollock (1912–56). Much has been said about them, with almost all the focus being on Pollock. A May auction made him the newest member of the $100 million club, and the 1991 Pulitzer Prize for Biography went to Jackson Pollock: An American Saga by Steven Naifeh and Gregory White. At 934 pages long, the book inspired the Hollywood film Pollock (2000), for which Marcia Gay Harden won Best Supporting Actress for her portrayal of Krasner.

Indeed, Krasner herself has been seen as a supporting character for too long. In 1981, Barbara Rose curated the exhibition “Krasner/Pollock: A Working Relationship” to undermine the dominant narrative that she was a second-tier artist and long-suffering helpmate to her legendary husband, proposing that their marriage was a complex, working partnership of artistic equals. But Rose never got Krasner out of Pollock’s shadow.

A show that pays more attention to Krasner than Pollock (she outlived him by 28 years), “Past Continuous” is more daring, nuanced, and expansive than previous attempts because, finally, it treats them as equals. The exhibition starts with footage, a panoramic view of their unheated, two-story, shingled house and studio on Long Island, overlayed with historic stills of Pollock, Krasner, their dog Gyp, and their tamed crow, Caw Caw. This is where Krasner and Pollock lived for nearly 11 years, until Pollock killed himself and one of his passengers, Edith Metzger, while driving drunk, injuring his girlfriend, Ruth Kligman, too. At the time, Krasner was in Europe, distancing herself from her husband’s drinking and philandering.

It was in this house, far from New York and his favorite watering hole, the Cedar Bar, that Pollock made his first storied drip paintings. He unrolled unprimed canvas onto the studio floor and worked horizontally, applying enamel and house paints with sticks and brushes but never touching the canvas. He was inspired to do this by the paintings of Janet Sobel (1893–1968), a self-taught Ukrainian-born artist. Her Milky Way (1945), which he saw at Peggy Guggenheim’s Art of This Century gallery in 1946, directly inspired his first drip painting, Galaxy , in 1947.

Just two years later, a headline in the widely popular LIFE magazine asked “Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?” elevating him from little-known abstract painter to overnight celebrity. Its four photographs showed Pollock as a brooding, hyper-masculine figure smoking a cigarette and wearing paint-splattered jeans. Krasner is not mentioned; he is portrayed as a solitary male genius.

Subverting that myth, the Met show ambitiously resets the history of Abstract Expressionism, going a long way to reveal the complexity of their artistic relationship. The first gallery presents Krasner’s collage works from the mid 1950s, when Pollock was at an artistic impasse and spiraling out of control. Until now, we’ve only ever gotten the lamentable tragedy of Pollock’s decline sans the triumph of Krasner’s emergence from his shadow.

This retelling proves that by the mid-’50s, Krasner is Pollock’s equal and deserved to be see on her own. In Bald Eagle (1955), Krasner collaged scraps of dark brown linen and unprimed canvas that she and Pollock discarded, including on the white shape in the middle of the painting that resembles a bird’s profile, where we see Pollock’s dripped black line. Incorporating work rejected by her and her husband, Krasner was reborn, like a phoenix, from the destruction.

It’s an apt metaphor for Krasner’s entire life and career. Beset with doubts and periods of blockage, Krasner had to find constantly ways to move on and pursue a trajectory that was all her own, all while facing Pollock’s larger-than-life. Before she ever met Pollock, Krasner wrote these lines from Arthur Rimbaud’s poem A Season in Hell on her studio wall:

To whom shall I hire myself out? What beast must I adore? What holy image is attacked? What hearts shall I break? What lie must I maintain? In what blood tread?

Constantly restless and one tough cookie, Krasner understood how hard it was to maintain one’s integrity as an artist.

After proposing that Krasner more than held her own, the curators take a more biographical approach, placing examples of their early work—from before they met—in the same gallery. It starts with his-and-hers self-portraits—Krasner’s, in graphite and crayon, (ca. 1929-30); Pollock’s, a muddy brown, moody impasto (ca. 1930–33)—and includes a selection of paintings from a group show they both exhibited in, “American and French Painting” (1942). Curated by the Russian émigré artist and theoretician John Graham, it saw Pollock and Krasner hung alongside Stuart Davis, Willem de Kooning, Picasso, and Henri Matisse. After seeing the show and not knowing who Pollock was, Krasner looked him up. The rest is history.

The exhibition is filled with highpoints, from Pollock’s lyrically expansive masterpiece, Number 1, 1950 (Lavender Mist), to the recreation of Krasner’s groundbreaking exhibition at the Stable Gallery in 1955, which led the critic Clement Greenberg to proclaim her “a major addition to the American art scene of the era.” He later declared that with drip painting, Pollock had gotten past Cubism (meaning Picasso) and made the first great American paintings. Although Greenberg suggested that Krasner had taken collage (again Picasso) into a new American territory, he stopped short of being as laudatory as he was for her husband. It was this hierarchical thinking (or glass ceiling) that Krasner crashed against throughout her career.

Using pieces she and Pollock destroyed, abandoned, or never finished, she created both a body of work all her own. In Blue Level and Desert Moon (both 1955), with their solid areas of blues and reds, respectively, Krasner constructed a vertical world that stood straight and sturdy, raw elements reaching beyond the painting’s top and bottom edges. The verticality of these works can be seen as an aspirational self-portrait in which destruction and rebirth are literally and metaphorically merged.

The latter rooms of the exhibition are dominated by Krasner, who moves into new territory, while Pollock makes a handful of one-of-a-kind paintings, such as Portrait and a Dream and The Deep (both 1953). In her smartly vulgar The Seasons (1957), which extends nearly 17 feet, Krasner returns to the subject of rebirth one year after Pollock’s death, depicting abundant forms resembling genitalia. That boldness continued right up to Past Continuous (1976), her last monumental collage made of charcoal drawings she made while studying with Hans Hofmann.

In the 20 years between, we see major works from every decade. Restless as ever, she kept doing something unexpected. Take Kufic (1965), a spare, contemplative painting whose title refers to the oldest style of Arabic calligraphy, underscoring Krasner’s long interest in writing and linear marks. Rising Green (1971) is another standout in her masterful career.

The exhibition culminates with the Future Indicative (1977), collaging Krasner’s figure drawings. Krasner, self-critical and never fully satisfied with what she had done, made multiple masterpieces in paint and collage that stand on their own and resemble none of her contemporaries. Finally, Krasner is recognized for her powerful contribution to American art.

article_text:
写真家・早川勝夫による「pendulum Art Book & Fine Art Photo Exhibition」が、11月13日から18日まで、せんだいメディアテークで開催される。雪によって風景が消え、再び現れる現象を通して、写真が持つ「固定する力」と、絶えず変化する世界との関係を見つめるプロジェクトだ。

「雪に風景が消え、また現れる」。本作の起点にあるのは、雪がもたらす圧倒的な美しさと、視界を奪われる恐ろしさだ。降り積もる雪は風景の輪郭を覆い、距離や奥行きを曖昧にする。さらにホワイトアウトのなかでは、そこに存在しているはずのものさえ見えなくなり、「何を見ているのか」という知覚そのものが揺らぎ始める。

早川はこうした雪の性質と、一瞬を一枚の像として定着させる写真の性質を対置する。確かな輪郭を持っていた世界が白の中へ溶け、やがて再び姿を現す。その「見える／見えない」「存在する／消失する」という往還を、早川は「存在の還流」と呼ぶ。タイトルの「pendulum＝振り子」も、固定と揺らぎ、可視と不可視、存在と消失のあいだを行き来する運動に由来している。

本展の特徴は、展示とアートブックを一つの作品として構想していることにもある。アートブック『pendulum』は全270ページに62点を収録し、半透明のトレーシングペーパーを採用。ページをめくると、前の写真の気配を残しながら次の像が透過して現れ、重なり、そして消えていく。「見る」「触れる」「めくる」「待つ」という行為そのものによって、写真に内在する時間を体験させる仕掛けだ。

一方、会場では62点の作品から32点を選び、5つの章の流れを再構成するように大判プリントで展示。アルポリック板にマウントした作品をフローティングフレームに収め、壁面に固定されながらもわずかに「浮遊」するような状態を生み出す。ページをめくることで時間の中に現れるアートブックと、身体を移動させながら空間の中で像と向き合う展示。二つの異なる体験を往還することで、「pendulum」の世界を立ち上げる。

アートブック『pendulum』は2026年12月、Inunicより刊行予定。

アット・ザ・ベンチ

劇場公開日： 2026年11月13日

解説・あらすじ

映像監督・写真家の奥山由之が自主制作で手がけ、東京・二子玉川の川沿いにある古ぼけたベンチを舞台に、人々の何気ない日常を切り取ったオムニバス長編映画。 川沿いの芝生にぽつんとたたずむ小さなベンチ。ある日の夕方、そのベンチには久々に再会した幼なじみの男女が座り、もどかしくも愛おしくて優しい言葉を交わす。その後もこの場所には、別れ話をするカップルとそこに割り込むおじさん、家出をしてホームレスになった姉と彼女を捜しに来た妹、ベンチの撤去を計画する役所の職員たちなど、さまざまな人たちがやって来る。 動画配信プラットフォーム・Vimeoで2023年9月30日に第1編、24年4月27日に第2編を無料公開して反響を呼んだ2本の短編に、新たに制作した3本の短編を加え、全5編のオムニバス長編作品として劇場公開。キャストには広瀬すず、仲野太賀、岸井ゆきの、岡山天音、荒川良々、今田美桜、森七菜、草彅剛、吉岡里帆、神木隆之介ら豪華な顔ぶれが集結した。

2024年製作／86分／G／日本 配給：SPOON 劇場公開日：2026年11月13日

その他の公開日：2024年11月15日（日本初公開）

久しぶりに映画をみて笑った。 ポスタービジュアルをみて、これは『ナイト・オン・ザ・プラネット』じゃんと思っていたが、案の定で、ジム・ジャームッシュ好きには堪らない作品だった。そして『ナイト・オン・ザ・プラネット』と同様、役者のよさが十全に現れている。 第2編で何回笑ったか分からないし、岡山天音の挟まれ具合と岸井ゆきのの愛すべき面倒くささが絶妙すぎた。私もあのベンチでスーパーのお寿司を食べるのはあり得ないと思いつつ、多分買ってこられたら一緒に食べるし、それでいいと思う。 本作の最大の功績は、広瀬すずの横顔をどこから狙うのがいいか、答えが導き出された点であろう。そして切り返しショットで浮かぶ仲野大賀のにやけ顔に、今、最高に楽しいんだろうなと私もにやついてしまった。

2024年11月23日

iPhoneアプリから投稿

鑑賞方法：映画館

ベンチを舞台にした、4人の脚本家による基本会話劇のオムニバス映画。 ひとつのベンチで脚本家によってこんなに色が変わるのがおもしろい。そして作品ep1-5まで役者陣が豪華すぎた。 特にep1と2は最高だった。 仲野太賀×広瀬すずの化学反応がこんなに良いとは思わなかった。幼馴染の絶妙な距離感や探り合いが甘酸っぱくて、応援したくなる男女を見事に会話劇で演じていた。 私も夕焼けのベンチであんな会話をしたい人生だった…笑 そして夕陽に照らされる広瀬すずの横顔の美しさと、優しい仲野太賀の笑顔の尊さよ…。 ただ個人的にep5は蛇足に感じた。あの絶妙な距離感で想像にお任せで終わらせて欲しかった。 ep2は私の好みのどこかバカリズム感がある、細かいけどわかるーと思わせられるカップルの会話劇。いやー岸井ゆきの×岡山天音良かったー。会話のリズム感も良いし、何度も笑ってしまった。最後にトドメで荒川良々さん出してくるの卑怯すぎる（褒めてる） ep3は今田美桜×森七菜の姉妹の怒鳴り合いの喧嘩。今田美桜こういう役初めて見た。喉大丈夫！？って思うぐらい始終怒鳴り叫んでてすごかった笑 今田美桜演じる姉の行動は、妹と同じで私は理解できなかったけれど、あの姉妹の感じはすごくよくわかる。私がああなった時、私の妹は来てくれるだろうかなんて考えてしまった。 ep4はちょっと今までが良すぎたため、見劣りしてしまった。途中までは面白かったけれど最後が微妙すぎた。草彅剛×吉岡里帆×神木隆之介ってすごい組み合わせだっただけに、ラストあれは勿体なさすぎないか？ ep4が少し微妙だったけれど、全体的にはとても満足感の高いオムニバス作品だった。
